transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen, Samir Patel, Lena Ortiz (Redwood) - Brian Thompson, Aisha Rahman, Marco Silva, Emily Park (Catalyst Health)

Summary: Align on benchmark methodology for runtime performance across environments. Discussed load generation, prompt sets, making apples-to-apples comparisons across quantized vs fp16, and KV cache/batching interactions.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick round of intros?
[00:07] Brian Thompson: Hey all, Brian here, CTO at Catalyst. we run several clinical NLP workloads, and the goal today is to understand how we compare Redwood hosted vs our expected VPC/on-prem flows.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Great, and on the Redwood side Samir will lead the benchmarking methodology. Samir?
[00:20] Samir Patel: Yeah thanks. overview: we want deterministic apples-to-apples tests. that means matching prompt set, tokenization, seq lengths, warmup behavior, and KV cache usage across runs. also capture both latency p50/p95/p99 and throughput under sustained load.
[00:34] Aisha Rahman: Quick Q: for KV cache, are you measuring cold-starts only or steady-state with cache warm? our workloads often hit long conversations with patient histories so cache matters a lot.
[00:45] Samir Patel: Good call. We propose two modes: cold-start (no KV cache) and warmed-run (simulate steady-state with prefix caching). We'll provide harness hooks to pre-seed KV entries for warmed runs - though on fully private infra the seeding step needs coordination.
[00:58] Marco Silva: For on-prem we have strict network egress limits and internal proxies; can the benchmarking agent run inside our VPC behind the proxy?
[01:05] Lena Ortiz: Yes, the load generator can be run from within your VPC or on a jump host. we have a local runner (python/Go) that mimics the hosted SDK calls and records per-request timings. it supports token-level logging if you enable verbose mode. small caveat - token-level logs can be noisy and increase overhead.
[01:22] Emily Park: For the prompt set we want to include short queries, medium context (250-512 tokens), and long contexts (1k-2k). we'll also include reranking prompts and streaming responses.
[01:31] Samir Patel: Perfect. Also recommend including paired paraphrases for quality comparison when we test quantized variants - quant can slightly degrade generation quality and we want to track that in evals.
[01:42] Brian Thompson: On metrics: p95 latency under peak, tail latency, and tokens/sec. Also cost per 1M tokens for hosted vs projected for Dedicated.
[01:50] Maya Chen: We'll surface cost models after pilot, but the benchmark harness will produce token counts and effective tokens/sec so you can run cost projection.
[01:58] Aisha Rahman: Another thing: model variants - will we compare identical model checkpoints? sometimes vendor-provided quant conversions change architecture shapes slightly which biases results.
[02:07] Samir Patel: We'll ensure the same base checkpoint is used when possible; for quantization we produce deterministic conversions (int8/4-bit) using the same quant pipeline. we'll note any operator substitutions. for vendor supplied conversions we will annotate differences in the results.
[02:22] Marco Silva: network jitter: even with the runner in VPC we see occasional spikes. how do you account for network noise vs runtime kernel issues?
[02:29] Samir Patel: We capture end-to-end timing and also per-stage timing: client->front-end, front-end->runtime scheduling, runtime inference, and token emission. On-prem runs can run the agent and capture local runtime metrics to separate network from compute. we'll provide a lightweight psutil-style collector for CPU/GPU utilization and network latencies.
[02:46] Lena Ortiz: Also recommended: use a load pattern that ramps rather than immediate saturation. e.g., linear ramp to target concurrency over 60-120s, hold for N minutes, then ramp down. that reduces transient cold-start noise.
[02:58] Emily Park: For batching, do you test dynamic batching thresholds vs fixed batch sizes? our concern is latency for short queries when batching is enabled.
[03:06] Samir Patel: We'll test both. Configurable params: max_batch_size, batch_timeout_ms, per-shard batching behavior. We'll benchmark short-query SLOs with batching disabled and then with tuned batch_timeout to show tradeoffs. often a small batch timeout (1-3ms) gets better throughput without large latency regressions.
[03:23] Brian Thompson: On quantization, we need to see quality regressions on our clinical prompts. how do you produce the eval?
[03:29] Samir Patel: Provide your prompt set and expected outputs or references; we'll run BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity and also human spot checks. we can produce a quality-delta report per prompt and a thresholding rule to decide acceptable degradation.
[03:41] Aisha Rahman: Is there a standard for warmup length for KV cache? sometimes warm caches take thousands of tokens to produce stable hit rates.
[03:49] Samir Patel: We'll simulate realistic conversation lengths; recommended warmup is to replay representative prefixes until per-key hit-rate stabilizes. we log KV hit ratios as part of the harness. for the workshop we'll show both short and long warmup scenarios.
[04:03] Maya Chen: Let me highlight the apples-to-apples checklist we use: same model checkpoint and tokenizer, identical prompt and pre/post processing, identical decoding params, control for batching and cache state, identical hardware profile (GPU type / vCPU counts), and consistent network placement.
[04:18] Marco Silva: Regarding hardware profile, we run A100xLarge on-prem but with slightly older drivers. would driver differences matter?
[04:25] Samir Patel: Drivers and CUDA versions matter. We'll record driver versions and note kernel-level fallbacks. if needed we can run small microbenchmarks to show baseline kernel performance.
[04:36] Emily Park: For streaming responses, measurement is tricky - do you measure first-token latency and last-token throughput?
[04:42] Lena Ortiz: Yes, we capture first-token latency, mean inter-token time, and overall completion time. streaming also interacts with batching and KV cache; we'll include that matrix in the report.
[04:55] Brian Thompson: For security - KMS integration for key wrapping and customer-managed keys is a blocker for us. we need to see the KMS flow and audit logs.
[05:03] Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. we'll attach the security checklist and our SOC2 / ISO references. Samir, can you make sure the security deck has the KMS flow?
[05:12] Samir Patel: Yep, will add an appendix showing KMS handshake, envelope encryption, and audit events mapping.
[05:18] Aisha Rahman: Can the benchmark harness redact PHI in logs? we need to avoid PII/PHI leaving our environment.
[05:24] Samir Patel: The harness supports local-only logging and can hash or redact tokens before sending logs out. for the pilot we recommend running the harness inside your VPC and sharing only aggregated metrics and sanitized samples.
[05:36] Maya Chen: Timeline: if you can provide prompt sets and network topology by next Friday (2026-04-10) we can spin up the first hosted vs VPC apples-to-apples run the week of 13th.
[05:45] Brian Thompson: That works. we'll aim to get Aisha's team to prepare the prompt bundle and distribution specs.
[05:50] Marco Silva: One more practical: how do you reconcile GPU memory differences when comparing quantized vs fp16? quantized models often fit bigger batch sizes; we should normalize by effective throughput, not just latency.
[05:59] Samir Patel: Agreed. We'll report both per-request latency and normalized throughput per GPU and per-dollar metrics where possible. For fairness, we'll include runs constrained to the same memory footprint and alternate runs maximizing throughput.
[06:12] Emily Park: Will you provide the raw logs and a reproducible notebook?
[06:17] Lena Ortiz: Yes, the deliverable includes raw csv logs, the harness repo, and a reproducible analysis notebook that recreates charts.
[06:25] Maya Chen: Let's recap next steps and owners. we've captured action items in the doc; Samir will drop the harness repo link and example scripts, Aisha provides prompts, Maya will schedule kickoff.
[06:36] Brian Thompson: sounds good. thanks everyone, excited to see the apples-to-apples numbers.
[06:40] Maya Chen: Thanks, meeting adjourned.

End of transcript.
